items.title: Louie Bellson — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I met Johnny Hodges, Duke, Ben Webster, Barney Bigard, Tricky Sam [Nanton], Lawrence Brown, all of them.

ctx.x: Was that the first time you met Duke Ellington?

No. The first time I met Duke was in my hometown, Moline, Illinois, when Duke’s band came to town to play the Illinois Theater. That’s a good memory, right? I feel ashamed to say this, but Herb Jeffries was with the band, and they wouldn’t let the band stay at the hotel. They had to sleep on their bunks on the train. They came on the train. Duke offered to pay for the whole floor of the hotel. They still wouldn’t let him stay there. Herb Jeffries and I talk about that all the time. I met Duke then. I met Ben…
just him and I. We left the trumpet player back – 10,000 choruses back. That’s how I met Duke – through Ben Webster.

items.title: Louie Bellson interviewed by Monk Rowe, Sarasota, Florida, April 12, 1996
items.q: Juan Tizol, Lawrence Brown, Tricky Sam.

ctx.x: What’s that, I just read a quote from Andre Previn, who said a thousand musicians can get together and play a chord that Stan Kenton wrote and all the arrangers know how to do that. And Duke Ellington writes something for three instruments and they play it and I don’t know what it is.

Well in harmony and in theory it’s really much easier to write for four voices or five voices. But to write for three voices and two voices, because he had three trombone players, and those three trombone players sounded like five or six of them sometimes. But I found after working with the band I discovered in a very short time that you could have Ellington’s band play an arrangement, and then have another choice band, maybe like a New York band or an L.A. band, all great musicians, playing the same chart, but…
Didn’t they play some of your first charts?
